preamble: Deaspiration of [pʰ] to plain [p]. In Ancient Greek it results from Grassmann's law, a dissimilation whereby the first of two aspirates in successive syllables loses aspiration; it shows up in reduplicated perfects of φ-initial roots and in inherited words such as παχύς 'thick' (PIE *bʰénǵʰus, with *bʰ > pʰ and then deaspiration before the following χ). Unconditioned loss of aspiration is found in Sinhala, which, unlike most Indo-Aryan languages, lost the aspirated series entirely in its inherited vocabulary (Pali puppha > Eḷu pupa 'flower'); this loss is often attributed to a South Dravidian substrate.

examples.to: πέφυκα péphūka 'I have grown, I am by nature'
examples.note: Grassmann's law: the reduplicating syllable loses aspiration before the aspirated root-initial φ.
Root-internal Grassmann's law: *bʰ became pʰ in Greek and then lost its aspiration before the aspirate χ of the next syllable; cognate Sanskrit bahú 'much'.
Unconditioned loss of aspiration (with degemination); Pali stands in for the Middle Indo-Aryan input. Aspirated letters survive in the Sinhala script only for Sanskrit and Pali loanwords.
